title: US firms report widespread algorithmic management alongside accountability and worker-protection concerns
source_unit: OECD employer-survey respondent reporting firm use and governance of software that instructs, monitors, or evaluates workers
geography: France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Spain, and the United States; US-specific rates retained where reported

denominator.unit: firms with 20 or more employees across six countries; mid-level manager or supervisor respondent per firm

observations.method: Representative OECD employer survey of firms across all sectors; respondents reported whether their firms provided 15 algorithmic-management tools in instruction, monitoring, and evaluation categories, perceived impacts, concerns, and governance measures.
observations.uncertainty: Employer-side reports measure firm adoption and manager perceptions, not worker exposure, realized job quality, causal effects, or the exact number of US firms in each reported weighted rate.
observations.subgroup: Country, tool category, and firms with 20 or more employees; manager/supervisor respondent perspective.
observations.counterinterpretation: A firm may provide a tool without using it for consequential decisions; adoption is not intensity, worker exposure, or reduced autonomy.

denominator.unit: US weighted employer-survey rate; country-specific respondent count is not shown in the public summary

at_least_one_algorithmic_management_tool.unit: percent of US firms reported by managers

ten_or_more_tools.unit: percent of US firms reported by managers

monitoring_tools.unit: percent of US firms reported by managers

evaluation_tools.unit: percent of US firms reported by managers

observations.method: OECD weighted country estimates from the employer survey; tools cover software that instructs, monitors, or evaluates workers and are not necessarily AI-powered.
observations.uncertainty: These are firm-level manager reports, not worker-level exposure or verified system logs. The survey's algorithmic-management category is broader than generative AI.
observations.subgroup: United States firms with 20 or more employees; tool-category and intensity comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: High provision may reflect administrative or scheduling tools with limited worker consequence; it does not establish surveillance intensity, discipline, pay changes, or bargaining loss.

observations.period: June–August 2024; monitoring content/tone in the United States

denominator.unit: US weighted employer-survey rate; country-specific respondent count is not shown in the public summary

monitor_conversation_call_email_content_.unit: percent of US firms reported by managers

european_comparator.unit: percent average reported in France, Germany, Italy, and Spain

observations.method: Country-weighted employer-survey comparison for one monitoring tool category; the category concerns content or tone of conversations, calls, or emails.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison is between firm-reported provision, not actual monitoring frequency, worker consent, data retention, or enforcement. Country legal and sector composition differ.
observations.counterinterpretation: A reported tool may support quality or compliance work rather than discipline; the estimate does not reveal who can inspect, contest, or delete the resulting record.

observations.period: June–August 2024; trustworthiness and governance among algorithmic-management users

denominator.unit: algorithmic-management-using firms; item-specific valid universes across six countries

users_with_worker_impact_concern.unit: share of managers reporting at least one concern

most_common_concern.value: unclear accountability for a wrong decision

other_concerns.value: difficulty following algorithmic logic and inadequate protection of physical and mental health

firms_with_at_least_one_governance_measu.unit: percent of firms reported by managers

worker_consultation.unit: share of firms reporting worker consultation as a governance measure

observations.method: Descriptive employer-survey responses among firms using algorithmic-management tools; governance measures include assessments, audits, guidelines, ethics roles, whistleblower/complaint channels, and worker or representative consultation.
observations.uncertainty: Concern and governance measures are self-reported and do not establish effectiveness, worker awareness, remedy, or independent audit quality; rounded language in the policy summary is retained.
observations.subgroup: Algorithmic-management users across the six-country survey; concern and governance item universes differ.
observations.counterinterpretation: A governance policy can exist without meaningful worker power, enforcement, or a channel that changes a decision; concern can coexist with continued adoption.

related_sources.claim: OECD publication identifier for the employer survey study.
Related OECD worker-consultation experiment; separate German manufacturing setting and outcome design.

boundary: This record measures employer-reported provision, perceived managerial effects, trustworthiness concerns, and governance measures in a six-country survey. It does not establish worker exposure, job quality, pay, autonomy, bargaining power, health effects, enforcement, remedy, or US political action. Algorithmic management is broader than generative AI.
